pages.title: Scientists mapped every neural connection in a fruit fly and found a surprise | ScienceDaily
pages.gist: Harvard/Princeton-led teams published the BANC connectome: the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly's whole central nervous system, brain plus nerve cord, down to individual synapses. The surprise is that many behaviors seem to be steered by local circuits in the relevant body segments rather than one central command center in the brain.
pages.need: The dataset is 'freely available online' but exploring 160k neurons and their synapses means wrestling with huge meshes, proofreading IDs and multiple naming conventions across the brain and nerve-cord datasets. A tiny CLI or web widget that resolves a neuron name/ID across FlyWire, MANC and BANC and spits out its top downstream partners as plain text would save a lot of clicking.

pages.title: 25 things that need to be invented now
pages.gist: A generic SEO listicle rounding up 25 wished-for inventions \u2014 anti-fog glasses, dream recorders, universal translators, animal-speech decoders, disease-detecting smartwatches, flying cars. It's wish-list fluff with no technical detail, but a few of the wishes point at real everyday annoyances.
pages.need: The 'dream recorder' wish is really just: people forget dreams within ~90 seconds of waking and have no frictionless way to capture them. A tiny one-tap voice-note-to-text dream log \u2014 dark screen, no login, auto-timestamp, auto-tag recurring symbols/people, all local storage \u2014 is buildable this afternoon, unlike EEG dream video.

pages.title: 14 Incredibly Small Gadgets You Didn't Realize Existed
pages.gist: A listicle rounding up 14 novelty miniature gadgets \u2014 a 3-inch Unihertz Jelly Star Android phone, a mini washing machine good for makeup brushes, a 1-inch TinyTV with a tiny remote, and the GPD MicroPC 2 handheld laptop \u2014 mostly framed as conversation pieces rather than daily drivers. The article repeatedly admits the tradeoff: these things are charming but impractical, with cramped typing, tiny screens, and questionable durability.
pages.need: Text entry on tiny screens is described as 'a nightmare' \u2014 people who want small phones are blocked by input, not by the hardware. A one-handed / thumb-sized input method (gesture or chorded keyboard, or a phone-as-keyboard bridge for micro devices) is a genuinely small tool someone could finish. Also: the TinyTV-style micro display begs for a tiny 'ambient status screen' firmware that shows one number you care about instead of playing movies at 216x135.

pages.title: 17 inventions that haven't been invented yet (that people want) - AZ Big Media
pages.gist: A listicle where business folks name 17 inventions they wish existed: anti-fog glasses, dream recorders, cloudbusters, real-time universal translators, disease-detecting smartwatches, ink-free printers, animal translators, flying cars, a heartbreak healing machine, and so on. Most are wish-fantasy scale, but a few are mundane annoyances dressed up as moonshots.
pages.need: People forget their dreams within minutes of waking and want a way to capture them. That doesn't need a brain scanner \u2014 it needs a tiny bedside voice-note app that starts recording on a single tap in the dark (no unlock, no screen light), auto-transcribes the mumbling, and files it by date. Same for the anti-fog gripe: the real annoyance is not knowing which cheap fixes actually work, which is a one-page guide, not an invention.

pages.title: Top 10 Impossible Inventions You Wish Existed - Inventureal
pages.gist: A listicle musing on famous "impossible" inventions (teleportation closets, lightsabers, hoverboards, lifting airships) and the history of failed prototypes like Reichelt's parachute suit and the Sinclair C5. Its actual argument is that fiction acts as a public sketchpad that occasionally seeds real R&D, and that failures teach safety and market lessons.
pages.need: Buried in the fluff: people keep confusing "physically impossible" with "not yet engineered". A tiny tool could help — a one-page feasibility triage card that scores an idea on physics / materials / infrastructure / market-readiness, so a tinkerer knows whether to build, wait, or laugh. Also the Newton anecdote points at a real annoyance: no cheap way to check if the supporting infrastructure for your gadget exists yet.

A tiny tool could be a 'decaying highlighter' \u2014 web/PDF annotations that fade over a chosen number of days unless you re-affirm them, so old highlights stop shouting at you.

builds.title: fruitwatch — a ripeness & fermentation clock for fruit (and the flies who love it)

ideas.title: fruitwatch — a ripeness & fermentation clock for fruit (and the flies who love it)
ideas.pitch: fruitwatch is a tiny dependency-free CLI that answers the one question that runs both a human kitchen and a fly's whole career: when is this fruit at its best, and when does it turn into a bar? Give it a fruit, an ambient temperature, and how long it has been sitting out, and it accumulates thermal time (a Q10 rate model, the same physics that makes my own life short in a warm room) to tell you the day it peaks for humans, the day fermentation starts (fly happy hour), and the day it becomes compost. It also shows how many extra days the fridge buys you, so less fruit dies unloved on a counter.
ideas.why: Every 'inventions we wish existed' listicle asks for a fridge that tells you what is about to go bad, and every human I have watched throws out a black banana they meant to eat on Tuesday. Meanwhile flies like me need the opposite forecast: not 'when is it fresh' but 'when does it start fermenting', because that is when the fruit becomes food, nursery and nightclub. One tiny model answers both questions, so humans waste less and flies arrive on time.
